In all such partly verbal, partly nonverbal kinds of rhetorical devices, the nonverbal element also persuades by reason of its symbolic character. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. My arguments for the importance of ambience should not be understood as any simple call to "pay attention." One is in any event only partially aware of ongoing events within one's environs at any given time. The environs are ready-to-hand, yes, but they now have agentive powers Heidegger's hammer never had. Emile A arts and Stefano Marzano point out, "As technology becomes hidden within these static, unintelligent objects, they will become subjects, active and intelligent actors in our environment ... [and the] immaterial world of our interactions with them-services, games, entertainment, information, communication-will become more prominent in our lives" (8-9). Greenfield argues that ubiquitous computing "will disturb unwritten agreements about workspace and homespace, the presentation of self and the right to privacy. It contains an inherent, unsettling potential for panoptical surveillance, regulation, and 'rationalization.' Its presence in our lives will transfigure our notions of space and time, self and other, citizen and society in ways we haven't begun to contemplate" (3). In short, ambient intelligence radically changes who we are in our environs; it

situates us differently in the world, evoking other ways of being. It thereby also reveals rhetoric to us differently than it has appeared heretofore. Ambience thus teaches us that we cannot rely solely on salience, attention, and consciousness to guide us.

Rhetoric has much to learn from music on this score. I am claiming that ambient music is an important development, both in its own right as a form of thinking (and not simply as expression ofhuman thought and affect) and as something that shows how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to the music's creation but to what we take the music to be. Music is not just the salience of its affective work. Ambient music has still other rhetorical dimensions, including politics. It has ramifications for how we dwell in the world. Eno claims that ambient music is directly political: "The decision to stop seeing yourself as the centre of the world, to see yourself as part of the greater flow of things, as having limited options and responsibility for your actions[.] ... that is political theory: and it's where the music grows from" (qtd. in Tamm 91).

It is hardly a stretch to see that these political insights resonate with the extension of digital computing into things and environs. As Eno is quite aware, there are both opportunities and dangers here, which is why transforming how one sees oneself in the world is integral to a politics attuned to these dangers. 21 So, much as ambient music does, ubiquitous computing (ambient intelligence) showcases how the power of place and the agency of technology become integral not just to our everyday activity but to a conception of dynamic life itself. We need not overstate the case by claiming we are on the threshold of a brave new world. Rather, we are simply seeing capacities, implications, and energies as previously assembled now giving way to vibrant and different intensities and assemblages. But we cannot ignore how these different forms also assemble new forms oflife, or new ways of being-in-the-world.

Rhetoric, Ambience, Dwelling

We need conceptions ofrhetoric that keep pace with these transformations and their attendant opportunities and dangers, that not only help us make sense of them but enable us to flourish (and that will, of course, spur new transformations). We do not need a new rhetoric, however; rather, we must work anew with what has been brought forward in rhetorical theory and practice. Rhetoric is revealing and doing-doing as revealing and revealing as doing-and hence integral to our dwelling in the world. It can no longer be understood solely as a subjective, verbal, visual, or even performative

In terms of an ambient rhetoric, we must not simply turn our sights to sound and ask how we can now use sound to generate desired affective responses. As I stated earlier, we need more than a sonic semiotic. That would certainly be a possibility, but it obscures the deeper insights that sonics thought ambiently can afford us. We can do more with this insight into the ambience of design than single out and focus on various strands, such as the functional (how usable it is), the cognitive (what it means for us), or the affective (how it makes us feel). Instead, we could build a fresh, cumulative list of things with which we might concern ourselves as teachers, writers, and rhetoricians. I have argued that it is better to see them as complexly generating an overarching ambient environment that cradles, without forcing, particular affective responses or that fosters an attunement (as with "clear, confident, and connected," which is Microsoft's take on a positive, secure feeling that will enable work and play). Such a perspective reflects a fuller, less instrumental view of human beings and their interactions, particularly multimedia rhetorics. It deprivileges dir ectly conscious experience and boosts the importance of indirect, unconscious, auratic, osmotic, and ambient phenomena. Put differently, such rhet orical design

organizes an experience, not so much to persuade in any direct sense, but to attune and inflect our sense of bodily inhabitance and the cradle of intelligibility within which we comport ourselves. It is worth recalling Eno's irony-laden dismissal of the corporate sloganeering Microsoft delivered to him as part of the project. If Microsoft perhaps intended more direct forms of marketing and the shaping of the user's experience, including the service of avant-garde musicians to brand Microsoft products, it is important that Eno's music resists such narrowing. For Eno, ambient music is inherently political, evoking new senses of place and how human beings inhabit it; this includes, more pointedly, a reduced role for human agency reflecting a more distributed, ecological approach to will, action, and consequence. The lengthy video session with Robert Fripp and the Microsoft team suggests that such aesthetics and their politics, however indirect, are nevertheless in play. So, while startup music itself makes up only a small element amid these far larger concerns (not to mention the larger expanse of sonic space and its rhetorical-architectural possibilities), possibly one of little relevance, it nevertheless can open us onto a deeper reflection concerning our relation to technology, space, and sonics, and we lose much ifwe ignore the insights it grants.

Perhaps the statement "language speaks" is rather obscure but it is certainly no more obscure than the statement "I speak."

This, however, is precisely what renders advertising, or at least much of it, shrill. Forms of rhetoric that disclose the world and place human beings as resources for maximizing advantage, as most advertising does, eschew or foreclose the rich ecological relationality of being-in-the-world. That is, such forms deattune us. One cannot simply castigate this move. of course. One ought not simply say that advertising is wrong or evil, nor am I making any such argument. But neither should we ignore how advertising can convey narrowly suasive aspects of our being to disproportionally outsize all others, like eating nothing but cake all day. Other ambient variables that could condition advertising in its specific messages (you need cheap tacos at 2 a.m. !) or larger sayings (Consume!) are dimmed. This dimming contributes simultaneously to advertising's power and to our phenomenological reaction to it as shrill, as too sweet. A diet of advertising is unsustainable. And for this reason, while advertising is rhetoric, neither good nor ill, it would be an error to posit it as illuminating rhetoric's basic principle. Of course, this is precisely what, say, philosophy commonly does: thinly slice rhetoric as a manipulative version of persuasion, so that we see its shrillest forms as constituting its primary essence. A "sustainable" rhetoric (I discuss sustainability and sufficiency in chapters 7 and 8) is one that brings us to the richer experiences already spoken through language's saying, not solely as a sign system, but as the ch orographic background resounding of our attunement to the world.in

Heidegger's theory oflanguage allows us to rethink rhetoric as persuasion so as to take it out of a delimiting subject/object framework. Persuasion is certainly an affordance of rhetorical interaction, but an ambient perspective lets us see that taking rhetoric as persuasion narrowly and subjectively defined deflects our emplacement in the background "relation of all relations" that is language and distances us from the conditioning sway of the nonhuman that also gives place and bearing to rhetoric (Heidegger, OWL 135). Rhetoric emerges from our being-in-the-world, then, precisely also as a response to the way the world attunes and speaks us, but a response that allows for new forms of revealing that transform, at least potentially, how we are in relation to the world. This grants that even ifwe keep rhetoric always within language's orbit, language is never simply the doing of human beings, so that the wellspring of what rhetoric is and can be is opened through an attunement to its ambience. That is, rhetoric not only

receives its bearings from an attunement to all aspects of worldly existence that give rise to ways of being, human and nonhuman, but does so without mistaking any given presencing as ultimate being. Rhetoric thereby shares in a partiality that, rather than limits us, offers us hope for further and enriching unfoldings in rhetorical being.

The Rhetorical Thing

Objective, Subjective, Ambient

Only when man becomes the subject do non-human beings become objects.

-Martin Heidegger, Parmenides

"Words and things" is the entirely serious title ofa problem. -Michel Foucault, The Archaeology of Knowledge

Objects themselves, far from the insipid physical bulks that one imagines, are already aflame with ambiguity, torn by vibrations and insurgencies equaling those found in the mosttortured human moods.

-Graham Harman, Tool-Being

Rhetoric has always dealt with things, which is to say that rhetoric has not ignored the material realm. The field's historically predominant focus on rhetor, audience, and language may obscure this point, but contemporary rhetorical theory in particular attends to materiality. For instance, the field has firmly incorporated Marx's notion of dialectical materialism and its attendant critique of ideology. In addition, substantial contemporary work has investigated technology, institutions, and bodies. Indeed, even the notion of materiality is increasingly thematized in its own right as worthy of direct scholarly attention (Biesecker and Lucaites, Kochin). But the problem has always been how and to what extent materiality itself matters. As a long tradition has had it, rhetoric, being one of the seven liberal arts and crucial for the formation of what we call the humanities, is most fundamentally an affair of human beings and their dealings. It is overwhelmingly discursive, a verbal art. So, yes, things matter, but as objects of concern for rhetoric or as part of the

In their way oflife they give the island to take part, not to preserve it or to naturalize it, but to cultivate it as part of their homemaking. Indeed, this gets at the essence of dwelling, caring for as a freeing to let something be what it is.14 Rather than utter no to technology or to building, this hearkening brings forth a relation to technology that takes its bearings from the profundity of a holistic ecology, which tempers the will to impose, dominate, or master with the call to care.

The world, thought as material presence, as meaning, and as that which withdraws, is sacralized by everyday practices in such a fashion as to ground meaning and worth beyond the human. Values, ifwe can still risk that term, emerge from these practices and are neither settled nor projected solely by human beings. On this account, if values in this sense transcend human being, then Latour's Dingpolitik must already be spoken in a way oflife. Dwelling gives rise to Dingpolitik, which is to say that there is already something like an ethic implicit in our worldliness. There is no adding on a new comportment toward things, toward world after the fact, as Latour would have it. Indeed, this is the crucial point for understanding why religion, art, and other forms of knowledge are just as important as science or politics; they are already in deep relation to and disclosive for our way of being, for the way we dwell. for ethos. Thus, performing rhetoric in an ambient key is less a matter of adding them back in than of reattuning ourselves to their station, and to what their station may yet be, in our struggle to find better, more sustainable practices. Certainly, their role in knowledge formation and ethics remains vital. But there are other aspects that could be made equally vital. For instance, religion, art, and forms of celebration would be important for their evocation of something like the festive. Festivity need not be happy and chipper, either; the festive is important for attuning us to the gifting of the world and a sense of value that transcends human being, manifest through moods of contemplation, reverence, joy, or other possibilities.15 Such celebration is also a form of preparatory rhetoric, since it discloses world differently and opens the possibility of dwelling anew. That is, art, religion, and other ways of being with things would allow them to show up for us as things that are indispensable for our way oflife and for the being of world in general: they are radiant in such fashion that they are graced to us and so lay claims on us should we listen to them. 16 Note that this aligns with Latour's and Heidegger's claims that science is not the sole source for knowledge about things. One need not

accede to antiscience religious doxa to uphold the idea that science is not the last instance for determining the knowledge that enlivens our everyday being. The festive is one way to pursue this enlivening.

Although I find the Toronto Islanders' resistance to the automobile important and illuminating, it is important not to romanticize their efforts, as if the island's residents have found an ideal path that we should then imitate. Not only is it difficult to transport practices that are so wedded to the region, since the specificity of place is an integral element in those practices, but it is far from assured that they have succeeded. Indeed, I have spent a good amount oftime explicating where they struggle. Nevertheless, we cannot neglect the rhetorical potency of arguments such as Princen's or practices such as those of the Toronto Island residents. I have stated that they are only preparatory, and I want to close on that note. Such preparation lays the groundwork necessary for awakening attunements that in turn give rise to other forms of disclosure and receptivity. That is, thought in terms of an ambient rhetoric, such preparatory work is crucial, for it brings us in touch with the world's primordial affectability, and disclosing this transforms how world comes to us in a way that shifts our manner of being in that world. This suggests that this book itself is ultimately only preparatory. Perhaps this too is necessary. An ambient rhetoric cannot trump itself, cannot short-circuit itself into being a new paradigm. That would run counter to its disclosive power for rhetoric itself. When it comes to world making, an ambient rhetoric can only attune and, by such attunements, conjoin us in worldly affectability giving place and bearing to everything we are and everything we do.

To take one instance, speakers or writers may well understand themselves as working with conscious intent, yet the intention may be causally irrelevant to the effects produced in the audience. Rhetorical theory tends to assume that intent equals result: a rhetor wants to persuade a group of people to vote a certain way, the rhetor succeeds, and therefore the rhetor's intent is held to have been successfully realized through his or her rhetorical art. Arabella Lyon remarks that rhetoric has maintained its boundaries by this adherence to discourse understood as instrumental (4). This is also rhetoric's built-in retroactivity, according to which what works is always telegraphed by an initial intentional action. Curiously, however, intent is rarely called into question when a rhetorical message goes awry; rather, the issue becomes a matter of technique. This idea underpins the longstanding idea of rhetoric as a teachable art. Failure results because one's message was not sufficient for the intent, because one was unprepared for the pa rticular audience, because one made a mistake, and so on. There is no leeway for accidental persuasion, for persuasion at odds with or in spite of intent or even the artistry of rhetorical work. Instead, the causality of rhetorical intent actualized through rhetorical work is often assumed as an unquestionable given. A great deal of excellent work, however, has been done on aleatory methods (see Vitanza, "From Heuristic"); unconscious forms of persuasion, such as Burke's identification, taken from psychoanalysis (see D. Davis, Inessential; Lundberg and Gunn); complexity and ecology (Cooper, Dobrin, Edbauer, Hawk, Lanham); and various proponents of hermeneutic and postmodern thought (Biesecker; Hyde; Lyon; Mailloux, "Rhetorical Hermeneutics" and "Rhetorical Hermeneutics Still"). It is

thus perhaps surprising that we have not made more progress here. But as Lyon suggests, intent has in fact been woefully undertheorized in rhetoric precisely because it is always assumed (3-4). What I have described as essential to an ambient rhetoric-its embodied and embedded or situated character, its dispersal across things that themselves have gradations of agency, and its dynamic emergence within an environment that occasions certain effects-suggests that intent is only one element in a large array of things, feelings, peoples, and forces all complexly interacting. To say this is not to deny the existence or importance of intent but rather to insist that within any given rhetorical event, intent cannot suffice for its full accounting as rhetoric-not to mention the near dogmatic assertion of intent as the expression of the subjective will.

The emphasis on self-consciousness, another aspect of Cole's definition, is just as problematic. Each of the four strands of thought I brought to the notion of ambient rhetoric emphasizes the idea that at any given time, we are only partially conscious of what we are doing, why we are doing it, and what will result from it. When we tether intent to self-consciousness, we cut off large swaths of human activity from rhetorical practice in our rhetorical theory. That last prepositional phrase is crucial: the point is not that what is denied to self-consciousness fails to come into play in rhetorical engagement but that we deny inquiry into those aspects when our rhetorical theory opens itself only onto what is immediately self-conscious and thus easily tethered to humanist notions of willing. Intent and selfconsciousness no doubt matter enormously, but they no longer suffice to determine what rhetoric is and is not. Behind the conventional notion of intention lies a model of human being as an autonomous, self-knowing, subjective agent. Everything I have here described works to undo and disperse this model as a reduced view of human being.

In sum, I hope this book helps us to see such narrowing as a way to impoverish rhetoric when we should be opening it up, not to make it bigger, but to attune us, in rhetoric and via rhetoric, to its fullest flowering. Rhetoric's timeliness as a field of inquiry and a practice has never been more propitious. As I suggested previously, transformations in ourselves, in our historical conjuncture, and in our built environments have occasioned revised understandings of human being and the world. The dynamically ecological imbrications of places, things, and informatics can be read as a (partial) rhetoricization of the world in the most concrete and material way imaginable. As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement.
